Paediatric Pneumonia Screening: Classical Machine Learning versus Deep Learning¶

Machine Learning (PCOM7E), Unit 11 Individual Presentation, Track A (Computer Vision).

Dataset: paediatric radiographs published by Kermany, Zhang and Goldbaum (2018); the DOI is given in the References.

The task is binary: decide from a paediatric chest radiograph whether pneumonia is present. Two models are built on exactly the same images and compared:

  1. Classical machine learning: histogram of oriented gradients (HOG) features with a radial basis function support vector machine (scikit-learn).
  2. Deep learning: a compact convolutional neural network trained from scratch (TensorFlow and Keras).

The notebook follows the order of the brief: dataset and preprocessing, model design, evaluation and validation, explainability and bias and diagnostic analysis, followed by deployment-relevant measurements and a demonstration. Ethical and deployment discussion is developed in the presentation itself.

Every figure used in the slides is written to assets/ by this notebook.

Dependencies¶

This notebook requires tensorflow, scikit-learn, scikit-image, lime, opencv-python, numpy, pandas and matplotlib. The versions used for the submitted run are printed by the first code cell (lime does not expose its version in code; version 0.2.0.1 was installed). To reproduce the run exactly: pip install tensorflow==2.21.0 scikit-learn==1.8.0 scikit-image==0.26.0 lime==0.2.0.1 opencv-python==4.10.0.84 numpy==2.4.6 pandas==2.2.3 matplotlib==3.10.8.

The image archive is not bundled with the notebook. Download ChestXRay2017.zip (about 1.2 GB) from the Mendeley Data record listed in the References and unzip it in the same folder as this notebook, which creates chest_xray/train and chest_xray/test. To keep the images elsewhere, set the environment variable CHEST_XRAY_DIR to the unzipped chest_xray folder before starting Jupyter. The first run caches the resized images in a cache/ folder beside the notebook, so later runs skip the slow decoding.

The archive arrives as JPEG files in train and test folders, each split into NORMAL and PNEUMONIA. The file names are the only record of patient identity: pneumonia files follow person<id>_<bacteria|virus>_<n> and normal files IM-<id>-<n>, sometimes with a further suffix, so the patient key is the person<id> or IM-<id> part of the name. Keying on the number alone treats a bacterial and a viral file with the same number as one child, which is the cautious choice for grouping. Images are read once, resized and cached as a NumPy archive so later runs skip the slow decoding.

In [2]:
def describeRadiograph(filePath, splitName):
    fileName = os.path.basename(filePath)
    classFolder = os.path.basename(os.path.dirname(filePath))
    if classFolder == "PNEUMONIA":
        nameParts = re.match(r"(person\d+)_(bacteria|virus)_", fileName)
        patientKey, subtypeName = nameParts.group(1), nameParts.group(2)
    else:
        patientKey, subtypeName = re.match(r"((?:NORMAL2-)?IM-\d+)-", fileName).group(1), "normal"
    return {
        "split": splitName,
        "path": filePath,
        "label": int(classFolder == "PNEUMONIA"),
        "subtype": subtypeName,
        "patient": f"{splitName}/{classFolder}/{patientKey}",
        "patientKey": patientKey,
    }


recordList = []
for splitName in ("train", "test"):
    for classFolder in ("NORMAL", "PNEUMONIA"):
        pattern = os.path.join(datasetRoot, splitName, classFolder, "*.jpeg")
        for filePath in sorted(glob.glob(pattern)):
            recordList.append(describeRadiograph(filePath, splitName))
catalogue = pdlib.DataFrame(recordList)

cacheFile = os.path.join(cacheFolder, f"radiographs-{imageSide}.npz")
if os.path.exists(cacheFile):
    cached = nplib.load(cacheFile)
    pixelStack, originalShapes = cached["pixels"], cached["shapes"]
else:
    pixelStack = nplib.zeros((len(catalogue), imageSide, imageSide), dtype=nplib.uint8)
    originalShapes = nplib.zeros((len(catalogue), 2), dtype=nplib.int32)
    for rowIndex, filePath in enumerate(catalogue["path"]):
        rawImage = cv2.imread(filePath, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
        originalShapes[rowIndex] = rawImage.shape
        pixelStack[rowIndex] = cv2.resize(rawImage, (imageSide, imageSide),
                                          interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
    nplib.savez_compressed(cacheFile, pixels=pixelStack, shapes=originalShapes)

catalogue["height"], catalogue["width"] = originalShapes[:, 0], originalShapes[:, 1]
catalogue["exposure"] = pixelStack.reshape(len(catalogue), -1).mean(axis=1)

print("Chest X-ray catalogue")
print(sectionRule)
print(pdlib.crosstab([catalogue["split"], catalogue["subtype"]], catalogue["label"],
                     margins=True).to_string())

1. Dataset Selection and Preprocessing¶

Why this dataset. It is the first example the brief names, it comes from a documented clinical source, a children's hospital in Guangzhou where two physicians graded every image (Kermany et al., 2018), it carries a CC BY 4.0 licence and it poses a decision where errors are unequal in cost: a missed bacterial pneumonia delays antibiotics, whereas a false alarm costs a second look.

Three points from this output shape everything that follows.

  • Class imbalance. Pneumonia makes up 74.2 per cent of the training images, so a model that always answers "pneumonia" would already look accurate. Recall, specificity and precision-recall measures are therefore reported alongside accuracy.
  • Repeated patients. Pneumonia patients contribute 2.36 images each on average and one child contributes 30. Folds that split images rather than children would let a model be scored on a child it has already seen.
  • An undocumented split. 170 pneumonia identifiers appear in both the training and test folders. The record documents patient independence only for its eye scans, so whether these are the same children cannot be confirmed. It is recorded as a provenance limitation rather than corrected.

Preprocessing keeps the two models on identical inputs up to the point where their designs diverge:

  • Greyscale, 128 x 128, scaled to 0-1. The originals range from 127 to 2,713 pixels tall. 128 pixels keeps the lung fields and broad opacities while making five-fold CNN training feasible on a CPU.
  • HOG for the classical model (Dalal and Triggs, 2005). Each image is divided into cells 16 pixels wide, cells are normalised in overlapping groups of four and edge directions are binned nine ways, which yields a vector of 1,764 numbers for every image describing where edges run and how strongly.
  • Class weights of 1.939 for normal and 0.674 for pneumonia make each class contribute equally to both models' training loss.
In [5]:

hogSettings = {"orientations": 9, "pixels_per_cell": (16, 16),

def gradientHistograms(imageBatch):
    return nplib.stack([hog(singleImage, **hogSettings) for singleImage in imageBatch])


startClock = time.perf_counter()
trainHog = gradientHistograms(trainPixels[..., 0])
testHog = gradientHistograms(testPixels[..., 0])
hogSeconds = time.perf_counter() - startClock

positiveShare = trainLabels.mean()
classWeights = {0: 0.5 / (1 - positiveShare), 1: 0.5 / positiveShare}

The HOG picture below shows what the classical model actually receives: not pixels, but a grid of dominant edge directions. Rib edges and the heart border are clearly encoded, which is why HOG can separate the classes at all, but diffuse haziness inside the lungs, the hallmark of consolidation, is only captured indirectly through weakened edges.

2. Model Design: Classical Machine Learning versus Deep Learning¶

Classical model. Standardised HOG features feed an RBF support vector machine with balanced class weights. The scikit-learn library is used because its pipeline refits the scaler inside every training fold (Pedregosa et al., 2011). The penalty C is the only tuned setting and is chosen by cross-validation from {1, 10}; gamma="scale" adapts the kernel width to the feature variance. The grid is deliberately narrow, since each value costs a full five-fold run, which is a limitation of this comparison. probability=True provides scores, so both models can be thresholded and ranked the same way. Those scores come from Platt scaling fitted on an internal split that scikit-learn does not group by patient, so the SVM's probabilities may carry a little within-patient optimism.

Deep model. Four 3 x 3 convolution layers (32, 64, 128 and 128 filters), the first three followed by group normalisation and 2 x 2 max pooling, then global average pooling, 30 per cent dropout and a sigmoid output. Doubling the filters as the maps shrink is the conventional pattern, and four layers at 128 pixels let each final unit see a large part of a lung while keeping the network to about 240,000 parameters, small enough to train five times on a CPU. Adam at its default rate of 0.001 with batches of 32 is a standard, stable starting point, and the rate is cut when progress stalls. Design decisions:

  • Trained from scratch, not transferred from ImageNet, so the comparison isolates learned versus hand-crafted features at a similar data budget.
  • Group rather than batch normalisation. During development, a run with batch normalisation collapsed in two of five folds, predicting pneumonia for every image even though its ranking of cases remained good. Epoch-by-epoch tracing showed smooth training loss but inference outputs swinging between extremes, because batch normalisation's running statistics lagged the weights. Group normalisation computes the same statistics in training and inference, and the collapse did not recur.
  • Augmentation by small rotations, zooms and shifts, but no flips: a mirrored chest places the heart on the wrong side.
  • Early stopping and learning-rate reduction monitored on an inner 10 per cent of patients held back inside each training fold, never on the fold being scored, with the best weights restored. At most 20 epochs. Early stopping only starts watching after six epochs: when it watched from the first epoch, two folds stopped after five and nine epochs with their best weights from epochs 1 and 5, before the network had learnt enough, because the small monitoring split makes its loss noisy. That run is kept in development/ as the record of the change, which was made on cross-validation evidence alone.
In [7]:
def buildSupportVectorModel(penaltyStrength):
    return make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        SVC(kernel="rbf", C=penaltyStrength, gamma="scale",
            class_weight="balanced", probability=True, random_state=888),
    )


def buildPneumoniaNet():
    netInput = keras.Input(shape=(imageSide, imageSide, 1))
    layerFlow = keras.layers.RandomRotation(0.02)(netInput)
    layerFlow = keras.layers.RandomZoom(0.1)(layerFlow)
    layerFlow = keras.layers.RandomTranslation(0.05, 0.05)(layerFlow)
    for filterCount in (32, 64, 128):
        layerFlow = keras.layers.Conv2D(filterCount, 3, padding="same", use_bias=False)(layerFlow)
        layerFlow = keras.layers.GroupNormalization(groups=8)(layerFlow)
        layerFlow = keras.layers.Activation("relu")(layerFlow)
        layerFlow = keras.layers.MaxPooling2D()(layerFlow)
    layerFlow = keras.layers.Conv2D(128, 3, padding="same", activation="relu",
                                    name="lastConv")(layerFlow)
    layerFlow = keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(layerFlow)
    layerFlow = keras.layers.Dropout(0.3)(layerFlow)
    netOutput = keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(layerFlow)
    pneumoniaNet = keras.Model(netInput, netOutput, name="pneumoniaNet")
    pneumoniaNet.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3),
                         loss="binary_crossentropy",
                         metrics=[keras.metrics.AUC(name="auc")])
    return pneumoniaNet


maxEpochs = 20
batchSize = 32


def trainPneumoniaNet(fitPixels, fitLabels, fitGroups, seedValue):
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(seedValue)
    innerSplitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.1, random_state=seedValue)
    learnRows, monitorRows = next(innerSplitter.split(fitPixels, fitLabels, groups=fitGroups))
    pneumoniaNet = buildPneumoniaNet()
    fitRecord = pneumoniaNet.fit(
        fitPixels[learnRows], fitLabels[learnRows],
        validation_data=(fitPixels[monitorRows], fitLabels[monitorRows]),
        epochs=maxEpochs, batch_size=batchSize, class_weight=classWeights, verbose=0,
        callbacks=[
            keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor="val_loss", factor=0.3, patience=2, min_lr=1e-5),
            keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=5, start_from_epoch=6,
                                          restore_best_weights=True),
        ],
    )
    return pneumoniaNet, pdlib.DataFrame(fitRecord.history)


previewNet = buildPneumoniaNet()
print(f"CNN parameters: {previewNet.count_params():,}")
previewNet.summary()

3. Measuring and Validating Performance¶

Generalisation, not training fit, is what matters for a screening tool, and a single train-validation split gives one noisy estimate that is easy to overfit by repeated tuning. Five-fold cross-validation gives five estimates and their spread. Two constraints shape the folds here:

  • Grouped by patient, so every image of a child sits in one fold.
  • Stratified, so each fold keeps the 74 per cent pneumonia share.

The out-of-fold predictions are used for two decisions only: the SVM's C and a recall-led threshold. The 624-image test set is never used for training or tuning: both models are final before it is scored, and the later explainability and bias analyses only describe those fixed models.

In [8]:
def scoreBinary(trueLabels, pneumoniaProbability, cutOff=0.5):
    predictedLabels = (pneumoniaProbability >= cutOff).astype(int)
    trueNeg, falsePos, falseNeg, truePos = confusion_matrix(trueLabels, predictedLabels,
                                                            labels=[0, 1]).ravel()
    return {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(trueLabels, predictedLabels),
        "precision": precision_score(trueLabels, predictedLabels, zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(trueLabels, predictedLabels),
        "specificity": trueNeg / (trueNeg + falsePos),
        "f1": f1_score(trueLabels, predictedLabels),
        "rocAuc": roc_auc_score(trueLabels, pneumoniaProbability),
        "prAuc": average_precision_score(trueLabels, pneumoniaProbability),
    }


patientFolds = list(StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=foldCount, shuffle=True, random_state=888)
                    .split(trainHog, trainLabels, groups=trainGroups))
imageFolds = list(StratifiedKFold(n_splits=foldCount, shuffle=True, random_state=888)
                  .split(trainHog, trainLabels))

leakedPatients = [len(set(trainGroups[fitRows]) & set(trainGroups[checkRows]))
                  for fitRows, checkRows in imageFolds]
print("Fold construction")
print(sectionRule)
print(f"patients split across fit and check rows, image-level folds:   {leakedPatients}")

      f"{[len(set(trainGroups[a]) & set(trainGroups[b])) for a, b in patientFolds]}")

The CNN folds are uneven in a revealing way. Every fold ranks cases well (ROC-AUC 0.928 to 0.993) and keeps specificity above 0.95, but at the 0.5 threshold folds 3 and 5 miss many pneumonias (recall 0.523 and 0.759). The network has learnt to separate the classes in every fold; what varies is where its probabilities sit, so a fixed 0.5 cut-off lands in a different place each time. Four folds also used the full 20 epochs, which suggests the network had not finished improving; a larger epoch budget is a reasonable extension.

In cross-validation the classical model leads on accuracy (0.977 against 0.855), recall (0.984 against 0.814), F1 (0.985 against 0.883) and ROC-AUC (0.997 against 0.973), with far smaller fold-to-fold spread; the CNN is ahead only on specificity and precision. On this evidence alone the SVM would be chosen. The authors' held-out test split below shows whether that ranking survives. The learning curves add a caution: in three folds the training and monitoring losses fall together, but in two (one of them fold 3, the run that stops at epoch 16) the monitoring loss levels off well above the training loss, a sign that those runs fit their own training children better than new ones. The noise in every monitoring curve reflects how small the inner split is (about 10 per cent of patients).

In [13]:
def thresholdForRecall(trueLabels, pneumoniaProbability, recallFloor=0.95):
    candidateCuts = nplib.unique(pneumoniaProbability)[::-1]
    for cutOff in candidateCuts:
        if recall_score(trueLabels, (pneumoniaProbability >= cutOff).astype(int)) >= recallFloor:
            return float(cutOff)
    return 0.5


svmCut = thresholdForRecall(trainLabels, svmOutOfFold[chosenPenalty])
cnnCut = thresholdForRecall(trainLabels, cnnOutOfFold)
print("Operating points chosen on out-of-fold training predictions (recall >= 0.95)")
print(sectionRule)
print(f"HOG + SVM threshold: {svmCut:.3f}")
print(f"CNN threshold:       {cnnCut:.3f}")

Operating points chosen on out-of-fold training predictions (recall >= 0.95)
**********************************************************
HOG + SVM threshold: 0.912
CNN threshold:       0.114

Final models and the untouched test set¶

Both final models are fitted to the whole training set (the CNN keeps its inner 10 per cent of patients for early stopping) and scored once on the test set. Two operating points are shown: the conventional 0.5, and the recall-led threshold chosen on out-of-fold training predictions to keep recall at or above 0.95.

Held-out test set (624 radiographs, never used for training or tuning)
**********************************************************
             HOG + SVM @0.5  CNN @0.5  HOG + SVM @0.91  CNN @0.11
accuracy              0.777     0.861            0.851      0.737
precision             0.738     0.839            0.819      0.708
recall                0.997     0.962            0.977      0.987
specificity           0.410     0.692            0.641      0.321
f1                    0.848     0.896            0.891      0.824
rocAuc                0.937     0.946            0.937      0.946
prAuc                 0.958     0.968            0.958      0.968

The cross-validation ranking reverses. On the test set the CNN is ahead at 0.5 on accuracy (0.861 against 0.777), F1 (0.896 against 0.848), specificity (0.692 against 0.410) and ROC-AUC (0.946 against 0.937). Both models lose much of their specificity: the SVM falls from 0.958 in cross-validation to 0.410, the CNN from 0.973 to 0.692. Recall does not fall (SVM 0.984 to 0.997, CNN 0.814 to 0.962). The test images are therefore not harder to diagnose as pneumonia; their normal images look different from the training normals, and both models read the difference as disease, the SVM far more than the CNN.

The published benchmark on this split is 92.8 per cent accuracy, 93.2 per cent sensitivity and 90.1 per cent specificity, from an ImageNet-pretrained Inception V3 (Kermany et al., 2018). Neither model here approaches its specificity, consistent with training from scratch at 128 pixels; a pretrained backbone is the obvious next comparison.

Thresholds do not transfer cleanly. The recall-led threshold for the SVM (0.912) improves its test accuracy to 0.851 and specificity to 0.641 while keeping recall at 0.977. The CNN's threshold (0.114) is pulled far below 0.5 by the two poorly calibrated folds, so on the test set it trades specificity down to 0.321 for recall of 0.987. A threshold tuned on one distribution is only a starting point on another.

In counts, at threshold 0.5: the SVM misses 1 of 390 pneumonia radiographs and flags 138 of 234 normal radiographs; the CNN misses 15 and flags 72. The precision-recall curve is shown beside the ROC curve because, on imbalanced data, it is the more informative of the two (Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015). The CNN's curves lie above the SVM's until recall passes about 0.95, so its test advantage is not an artefact of the 0.5 threshold; only at recall near 1.0 does the SVM hold precision slightly better.

4. Explainability¶

Two techniques are applied:

  • Grad-CAM (CNN only) asks how sensitive the predicted class score is to each channel of the last convolutional layer, uses those sensitivities to combine the channels and so produces a coarse 16 x 16 heat map of the regions behind the decision (Selvaraju et al., 2017).
  • LIME (both models) perturbs an image by switching superpixels off, fits a local linear model to the predictions and reports which regions moved the score (Ribeiro, Singh and Guestrin, 2016). Being model-agnostic, it is the one technique here that can place the SVM and CNN side by side.

A simple quantitative check accompanies the pictures: the share of each map that falls in the outer eighth of the image, where labels, markers and soft tissue lie, compared with that border's 43.8 per cent share of the area.

In [16]:
def gradCamHeatmap(radiograph):
    camModel = keras.Model(finalNet.input,
                           [finalNet.get_layer("lastConv").output, finalNet.output])
    with tflib.GradientTape() as gradientTape:
        featureMaps, pneumoniaScore = camModel(radiograph[None, ...], training=False)
        targetScore = pneumoniaScore[:, 0] if float(pneumoniaScore[0, 0]) >= 0.5 else 1 - pneumoniaScore[:, 0]
    channelGradients = gradientTape.gradient(targetScore, featureMaps)
    channelWeights = tflib.reduce_mean(channelGradients, axis=(1, 2))
    coarseMap = tflib.nn.relu(tflib.reduce_sum(featureMaps[0] * channelWeights[0], axis=-1)).numpy()
    if coarseMap.max() > 0:
        coarseMap = coarseMap / coarseMap.max()
    return cv2.resize(coarseMap, (imageSide, imageSide), interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)


borderWidth = imageSide // 8
borderMask = nplib.ones((imageSide, imageSide), dtype=bool)
borderMask[borderWidth:-borderWidth, borderWidth:-borderWidth] = False


def borderShare(heatmap):
    totalMass = heatmap.sum()
    return float(heatmap[borderMask].sum() / totalMass) if totalMass > 0 else nplib.nan


testCams = nplib.stack([gradCamHeatmap(testPixels[rowIndex]) for rowIndex in range(len(testPixels))])
cnnTestCalls = (cnnTestProbability >= 0.5).astype(int)
camBorder = nplib.array([borderShare(heatmap) for heatmap in testCams])

print("Grad-CAM attention outside the central lung window (outer 1/8 border)")
print(sectionRule)
print(f"border share of image area:              {borderMask.mean():.3f}")
print(f"mean border share of Grad-CAM, correct:  {nplib.nanmean(camBorder[cnnTestCalls == testLabels]):.3f}")
print(f"mean border share of Grad-CAM, incorrect: {nplib.nanmean(camBorder[cnnTestCalls != testLabels]):.3f}")

The pictures qualify that reassurance. Averaged over the pneumonia films, the heat maps concentrate on the central mediastinum, the heart and great vessels; averaged over the normal films, on the shoulders and the diaphragm. Neither average sits on the lung fields where consolidation appears. (Each map explains the class predicted at 0.5, so the normal-film average also contains the 72 false alarms.) The true-negative and false-negative examples draw attention to the shoulders and neck, next to the "R" laterality marker. Attention that is central is not the same as attention that is clinically meaningful.

In [18]:
limeExplainer = lime_image.LimeImageExplainer(random_state=888)


def segmentRadiograph(rgbImage):
    return slic(rgbImage, n_segments=64, compactness=10, start_label=0,
                channel_axis=-1)


def svmBatchProbabilities(rgbBatch):
    pneumoniaProbability = finalSvm.predict_proba(gradientHistograms(rgbBatch[..., 0]))[:, 1]
    return nplib.column_stack([1 - pneumoniaProbability, pneumoniaProbability])


def cnnBatchProbabilities(rgbBatch):
    pneumoniaProbability = finalNet.predict(rgbBatch[..., :1], verbose=0, batch_size=256).ravel()
    return nplib.column_stack([1 - pneumoniaProbability, pneumoniaProbability])


def limeImportanceMap(radiograph, probabilityFunction, sampleCount=1000):
    rgbImage = nplib.repeat(radiograph, 3, axis=-1).astype("float64")
    explanation = limeExplainer.explain_instance(
        rgbImage, probabilityFunction, labels=(1,), top_labels=None, hide_color=0,
        num_samples=sampleCount, segmentation_fn=segmentRadiograph,
        batch_size=200, random_seed=888)
    pixelMap = nplib.zeros(explanation.segments.shape)
    for segmentId, segmentWeight in explanation.local_exp[1]:
        pixelMap[explanation.segments == segmentId] = abs(segmentWeight)
    return pixelMap / pixelMap.sum() if pixelMap.sum() > 0 else pixelMap


limeSampler = nplib.random.default_rng(888)
limeRows = nplib.concatenate([
    limeSampler.choice(nplib.flatnonzero(testLabels == 1), 20, replace=False),
    limeSampler.choice(nplib.flatnonzero(testLabels == 0), 20, replace=False),
])

startClock = time.perf_counter()
svmLimeMaps = nplib.stack([limeImportanceMap(testPixels[rowIndex], svmBatchProbabilities)
                           for rowIndex in limeRows])
cnnLimeMaps = nplib.stack([limeImportanceMap(testPixels[rowIndex], cnnBatchProbabilities)
                           for rowIndex in limeRows])
limeSeconds = time.perf_counter() - startClock
segmentCounts = [len(nplib.unique(segmentRadiograph(nplib.repeat(testPixels[rowIndex], 3, axis=-1)
                                                    .astype("float64")))) for rowIndex in limeRows]

print(f"LIME on {len(limeRows)} test radiographs per model ({limeSeconds / 60:.1f} min)")
print(sectionRule)
print(f"superpixels per image: median {int(nplib.median(segmentCounts))}, "
      f"range {min(segmentCounts)} to {max(segmentCounts)}")
print(f"border share of LIME importance, HOG + SVM: {nplib.mean([borderShare(m) for m in svmLimeMaps]):.3f}")
print(f"border share of LIME importance, CNN:       {nplib.mean([borderShare(m) for m in cnnLimeMaps]):.3f}")
print(f"border share of image area:                 {borderMask.mean():.3f}")

LIME on 40 test radiographs per model (3.0 min)
**********************************************************
superpixels per image: median 56, range 45 to 62
border share of LIME importance, HOG + SVM: 0.358
border share of LIME importance, CNN:       0.421
border share of image area:                 0.438

With about 56 superpixels per image, fine enough to separate the lung fields from the mediastinum, LIME places 35.8 per cent of the SVM's importance in the border but 42.1 per cent of the CNN's, close to the 43.8 per cent area share. The mean maps below show why: the SVM's importance lies over the lung fields, strongest at the lower outer edge of the image-right lung, whereas the CNN's concentrates at the lower edge of the film, below the diaphragm. LIME therefore disagrees with Grad-CAM about the CNN, which points to the mediastinum. Two explanation methods giving different accounts of one model is itself a finding: neither picture can be taken as proof of what the network has learnt.

renderAndSave(figureHandle, "lime-comparison")

5. Bias and Diagnostic Analysis¶

The brief asks for performance disparities across subgroups. The dataset holds no sex, ethnicity or socioeconomic information, so two attributes that can be derived from the data are examined: pneumonia subtype (bacterial or viral) and image exposure, the mean pixel brightness, which is this dataset's equivalent of the lighting conditions the brief gives as an example. Exposure quartiles are cut on the training data. Wilson 95 per cent intervals are shown because several subgroups hold fewer than 100 images.

In [20]:
def wilsonInterval(successCount, trialCount, zValue=1.96):
    if trialCount == 0:
        return (nplib.nan, nplib.nan)
    observed = successCount / trialCount
    centre = (observed + zValue ** 2 / (2 * trialCount)) / (1 + zValue ** 2 / trialCount)
    halfWidth = zValue * nplib.sqrt(observed * (1 - observed) / trialCount
                                    + zValue ** 2 / (4 * trialCount ** 2)) / (1 + zValue ** 2 / trialCount)
    return (centre - halfWidth, centre + halfWidth)


exposureCuts = nplib.quantile(trainFrame["exposure"], [0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
testFrame["exposureBand"] = pdlib.cut(
    testFrame["exposure"], [-nplib.inf, *exposureCuts, nplib.inf],
    labels=["Q1 darkest", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 brightest"])
testFrame["svmCall"] = (svmTestProbability >= 0.5).astype(int)
testFrame["cnnCall"] = cnnTestCalls

subgroupRows = []
for groupColumn in ("subtype", "exposureBand"):
    for groupValue, groupSlice in testFrame.groupby(groupColumn, observed=True):
        for modelName, callColumn in (("HOG + SVM", "svmCall"), ("CNN", "cnnCall")):
            positives = groupSlice[groupSlice["label"] == 1]
            negatives = groupSlice[groupSlice["label"] == 0]
            recallHits, specificityHits = int(positives[callColumn].sum()), int((negatives[callColumn] == 0).sum())
            recallBounds = wilsonInterval(recallHits, len(positives))
            specificityBounds = wilsonInterval(specificityHits, len(negatives))
            subgroupRows.append({
                "attribute": groupColumn, "group": groupValue, "model": modelName,
                "pneumonia n": len(positives),
                "recall": recallHits / len(positives) if len(positives) else nplib.nan,
                "recall 95% CI": f"{recallBounds[0]:.2f}-{recallBounds[1]:.2f}" if len(positives) else "",
                "recallLow": recallBounds[0], "recallHigh": recallBounds[1],
                "normal n": len(negatives),
                "specificity": specificityHits / len(negatives) if len(negatives) else nplib.nan,
                "specificity 95% CI": f"{specificityBounds[0]:.2f}-{specificityBounds[1]:.2f}" if len(negatives) else "",
                "specificityLow": specificityBounds[0], "specificityHigh": specificityBounds[1],
            })
subgroupTable = pdlib.DataFrame(subgroupRows)

print("Subgroup performance on the test set (threshold 0.5)")
print(sectionRule)
print(f"exposure quartile cut points from training data (mean pixel value 0-255): {nplib.round(exposureCuts, 1)}")
print()
print(subgroupTable.drop(columns=["recallLow", "recallHigh", "specificityLow", "specificityHigh"])
      .round(3).to_string(index=False))

Subtype. At threshold 0.5 neither model shows a meaningful subtype gap: CNN recall is 0.971 for bacterial and 0.946 for viral pneumonia, with overlapping intervals, and the SVM misses only one case in total. This matters clinically, because bacterial cases are the ones needing urgent antibiotics.

Exposure. Recall stays at or above 0.944 in every quartile for both models. Specificity is where any disparity sits: the SVM falls steadily from 0.473 on the darkest normal images to 0.383 on the brightest, while the CNN peaks in the middle quartiles (0.724 and 0.754) and is lowest at both extremes (0.655 and 0.633). The intervals overlap, so this is a pattern to monitor rather than a proven bias.

Exposure barely differs between classes (medians 122.1 and 123.2 in training), so brightness cannot by itself explain the test-set collapse in specificity. The next diagnostic examines how the images were acquired.

An acquisition shortcut¶

Image geometry turned out to be the stronger signal. If a model can tell the classes apart from how the image was stored rather than what it shows, that is a shortcut, the kind of confounding Zech et al. (2018) found when CNNs learned to recognise the hospital a radiograph came from.

In [22]:

The shortcut is real. Normal radiographs were stored at about 1.7 times the height in pixels of pneumonia ones (median height 1,325 against 776 pixels) and with a squarer shape (aspect 1.22 against 1.49 in training). A logistic regression given only height, width and aspect ratio, with no pixels at all, reaches 0.834 accuracy in patient-grouped cross-validation, against 0.742 for always predicting pneumonia, and 0.829 on the test set, above the SVM (0.777) and within about three points of the CNN (0.861) at threshold 0.5, against 0.625 for always predicting pneumonia there. In addition, the test normals are wider than the training normals (aspect 1.35 against 1.22), which moves them towards the pneumonia shape.

In [23]:
testFrame["aspect"] = testFrame["width"] / testFrame["height"]
normalTest = testFrame[testFrame["label"] == 0].copy()
normalTest["aspectBand"] = pdlib.qcut(normalTest["aspect"], 3, labels=["squarer", "middle", "wider"])


def centreSquare(filePath):
    rawImage = cv2.imread(filePath, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    shortSide = min(rawImage.shape)
    topEdge, leftEdge = (rawImage.shape[0] - shortSide) // 2, (rawImage.shape[1] - shortSide) // 2
    squareImage = rawImage[topEdge:topEdge + shortSide, leftEdge:leftEdge + shortSide]
    return cv2.resize(squareImage, (imageSide, imageSide), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA) / 255.0


croppedHog = gradientHistograms(nplib.stack([centreSquare(filePath) for filePath in catalogue["path"]]))
croppedSvm = buildSupportVectorModel(chosenPenalty).fit(croppedHog[trainMask], trainLabels)
croppedTestProbability = croppedSvm.predict_proba(croppedHog[testMask])[:, 1]

    images=("aspect", "size"), medianAspect=("aspect", "median"),

                                      in zip(bandSummary.index, bandSummary["medianAspect"])])

**********************************************************
            images  medianAspect  svmFalseAlarm  cnnFalseAlarm  croppedSvmFalseAlarm
aspectBand                                                                          
squarer         78         1.156          0.333          0.154                 0.269
middle          78         1.353          0.603          0.192                 0.564

centre-cropped SVM on the full test set: {'accuracy': 0.796, 'precision': 0.755, 'recall': 0.997, 'specificity': np.float64(0.462), 'f1': 0.86, 'rocAuc': 0.917, 'prAuc': 0.939}

Both models track the shortcut. Among normal test images, false alarms climb with aspect ratio: for the SVM from 0.333 to 0.603 to 0.833 across the three thirds, for the CNN from 0.154 to 0.192 to 0.577. The CNN is less affected in every band, which is consistent with its better test specificity.

Removing the stretch does not remove it. Centre-cropping every image to a square before resizing, so that no geometric distortion survives, leaves the SVM's pattern almost unchanged (0.269, 0.564, 0.782) and lowers its test ROC-AUC to 0.917. The aspect ratio is therefore a marker of how the images were acquired, and whatever accompanies that acquisition (resolution, positioning, equipment) remains in the pixels. A plausible reason the SVM is more exposed, offered as a hypothesis rather than a tested result, is that HOG summarises global edge statistics, which such acquisition differences alter directly, whereas the CNN's zoom and shift augmentation and its pooling make it less sensitive to them. This is the kind of shortcut learning, reliance on spurious associations that generalise poorly, that Brown et al. (2023) link to unequal performance across patient groups. A preprocessing step cannot correct a confound in data collection; only validation on, and data from, other sites and devices can address it, as Zech et al. (2018) found for hospital systems.

6. Deployment Footprint and Demonstration¶

Deployment cost is measured on CPU, one image at a time for both models, as an inference API would receive them.

Deployment footprint (CPU, one image at a time)
**********************************************************
HOG + SVM: 1147 support vectors x 1764 features = 2,023,308 stored values, 2.1 ms per image
CNN:       240,609 parameters, 14.8 ms per image

The SVM is about seven times faster per image (2.1 against 14.8 ms) but its stored model is larger, because an RBF SVM must keep its 1,147 support vectors of 1,764 features each. Both are far below any latency that would matter in a radiology workflow, so speed does not decide between them.

The demonstration below screens one unseen test radiograph end to end, from JPEG to both models' scores and a Grad-CAM map. The image is chosen programmatically as the first pneumonia case on which the two models disagree.

In [25]:
def screenRadiograph(imagePath):
    rawImage = cv2.imread(imagePath, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    resizedImage = cv2.resize(rawImage, (imageSide, imageSide), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
    modelInput = (resizedImage.astype("float32") / 255.0)[..., None]
    svmScore = float(finalSvm.predict_proba(gradientHistograms(modelInput[None, ..., 0]))[0, 1])
    cnnScore = float(finalNet.predict(modelInput[None, ...], verbose=0)[0, 0])
    figureHandle, axisArray = pltlib.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 3.6))
    axisArray[0].imshow(resizedImage, cmap="gray")
    axisArray[0].set_title(os.path.basename(imagePath), fontsize=9)
    axisArray[1].imshow(resizedImage, cmap="gray")
    axisArray[1].imshow(gradCamHeatmap(modelInput), cmap="jet", alpha=0.4)
    axisArray[1].set_title(f"CNN Grad-CAM, p(pneumonia)={cnnScore:.2f}", fontsize=9)
    for axisHandle in axisArray:
        axisHandle.axis("off")
    pltlib.tight_layout()
    return figureHandle, {"HOG + SVM": round(svmScore, 3), "CNN": round(cnnScore, 3)}


disagreementRows = nplib.flatnonzero((testFrame["svmCall"] != testFrame["cnnCall"]).to_numpy()
                                     & (testLabels == 1))
demoRow = int(disagreementRows[0]) if len(disagreementRows) else 0
demoFigure, demoScores = screenRadiograph(testFrame.loc[demoRow, "path"])
print(f"true label: {'pneumonia' if testLabels[demoRow] else 'normal'} ({testFrame.loc[demoRow, 'subtype']})")
print(f"model scores: {demoScores}")
renderAndSave(demoFigure, "demo-screening")

true label: pneumonia (bacteria)
model scores: {'HOG + SVM': 1.0, 'CNN': 0.254}

The demonstration case is a bacterial pneumonia that the SVM flags with near-certainty (1.000) and the CNN misses at 0.5 (0.254). It illustrates why a single fixed threshold is a weak safeguard: at its recall-led threshold of 0.114 the CNN would have flagged it.

Both final models are saved so that demonstration.ipynb can demonstrate them without retraining.

Summary of Findings¶

Measure HOG + SVM CNN Geometry only (no pixels)
Cross-validation accuracy 0.977 0.855 0.834
Cross-validation ROC-AUC 0.997 0.973
Test accuracy at 0.5 0.777 0.861 0.829
Test specificity at 0.5 0.410 0.692
Test F1 at 0.5 0.848 0.896
Test ROC-AUC 0.937 0.946
  • Validation. Patient-grouped cross-validation favours the SVM, but the authors' held-out test set favours the CNN. Cross-validation on this dataset is optimistic for both models, because the training normals and the test normals were evidently acquired differently.
  • Calibration. The CNN separates the classes in every fold, but where its probabilities sit varies from fold to fold, so any fixed threshold, including the recall-led one chosen here, transfers poorly.
  • Explainability. Grad-CAM shows central attention on the mediastinum rather than the lung fields, and LIME places the CNN's importance low on the film; the two methods do not agree, so neither is taken as proof.
  • Shortcut. Image geometry alone predicts the label at 0.829 on the test set, above the SVM and close to the CNN, and false alarms on normal films rise with aspect ratio for both models, higher for the SVM in every band.
  • Limitations. One hospital, one age band, a two-value grid for C, a 20-epoch cap that four CNN folds reached, ungrouped Platt scaling inside the SVM and 170 pneumonia identifiers shared between the authors' training and test folders.
